children: Power infrastructure in some regions is struggling to meet booming AI-led demand for data centers, with investment increasingly directed to areas where electricity supply is more reliable, according to PwC's global infrastructure leader.
"Availability of power is probably one of the constraining factors as you look across the world," Clara Cutajar said in an interview.

"Data centers have accelerated that need [for power] pretty significantly, and the networks and the infrastructure related to electricity is probably not keeping up with the pace of the demand at this stage," she said.

The global race to offer new artificial-intelligence tools has led to a surge in data-center construction projects around the world. But the capital flows for those projects aren't equal in geographic distribution.

The Americas region is set to attract an outsized share of global data center investment relative to its economic output, with the U.S. key to the advanced-chip ecosystem, according to the PwC Global Data Centre Outlook 2026-50 report. The region accounts for an estimated $16.5 trillion in accumulated capital expenditures through 2050, with the U.S. alone responsible for $15.1 trillion, it said.

Meanwhile, Europe's $5.6 trillion in cumulative capex underperforms relative to the region's share of global gross domestic product. The region's self-inflicted constraints are weighing on AI infrastructure investment, the report said.

Power constraints, planning friction, and fragmented regulation across countries explain limited acceleration in investment. For example, a 2025 ban by the city of Amsterdam on new centers, citing land and grid limits, is "illustrative rather than exceptional," the authors said.

Building a data center is one part of the equation, but access to power is the other critical piece, Cutajar said. In countries where regulatory frameworks and policy guidelines are much more aligned and connections to the power grid can be established quickly, capital investment flows much more easily than in countries where there is a backlog of requests for power connections, she said.
"You can see capital start to shift potentially to parts of the world where the power equation is easier to solve," Cutajar said.
Meanwhile, more countries are considering regulations around data and privacy, making sovereignty another factor affecting where capital is invested and data centers are built, she said.

In July, the European Union launched a call for tenders to establish up to seven AI gigafactories to boost Europe's computing capacity, which could entail more than 30 billion euros ($34.78 billion) in investment. The gigafactories will incorporate advanced AI processors, software and cloud technology stacks, high-speed connectivity and energy-efficient data centers.

"If countries want data centers in their own backyard and they don't want to rely on connections to other countries, then that obviously will mean that more capital will flow into certain countries as well," Cutajar said.
